required_recommendations: Establish last known well (before the headache, dizziness and blurred vision began, about 18 hours before arrival) and the NIHSS (22).

IV thrombolysis: do not give, because last known well is about 18 hours before arrival, beyond the 4.5-hour window. Thrombectomy: proceed for the basilar artery occlusion (within 24 hours of symptom onset, NIHSS 22, pre-stroke mRS 0, PC-ASPECTS 7); pregnancy is not a reason to withhold it (ESO 2022; AHA 2026 maternal stroke statement).

Proceed to mechanical thrombectomy for the basilar artery occlusion without delay, with abdominal shielding and the lowest practicable fluoroscopy dose; keep blood pressure at or below 185/110 mmHg before the procedure, avoid hypotension (placental perfusion), and do not target systolic below 140 mmHg after successful recanalization.

Involve maternal-fetal medicine and obstetric anaesthesia from arrival without delaying thrombectomy: fetal heart check before and after the procedure, and an airway and sedation plan for an obtunded patient (GCS 10) who has been vomiting.
Admit to a stroke unit or neurocritical care with continuous cardiac monitoring (telemetry) for at least the first 24 hours, with frequent neurological checks for reocclusion and brainstem swelling.
Correct the sodium of 128 mEq/L with isotonic saline after the vomiting, avoid hypotonic fluids, and limit the rise to 8 mEq/L in 24 hours.

Start low-dose aspirin (81 to 150 mg daily) once imaging 24 hours after thrombectomy excludes haemorrhage; it is safe in the second trimester. Use therapeutic LMWH instead only if a cardioembolic source, venous thrombosis or a thrombophilia that requires anticoagulation is found. Do not use warfarin, a DOAC or a statin in pregnancy (ESO 2022).

Give venous thromboembolism prophylaxis while she is immobile (pregnancy and stroke): intermittent pneumatic compression at once, and prophylactic-dose LMWH once follow-up imaging excludes haemorrhage.
Use MRI without gadolinium for any further brain imaging.
After the acute phase, complete the work-up: agitated-saline echocardiography for a right-to-left shunt (hypermobile interatrial septum on TTE), and repeat protein C and S activity after delivery.

key_clinical_evidence: Last known well is before the headache, dizziness and blurred vision began, about 18 hours before arrival; the decline in responsiveness and the left hemiparesis 6 hours before arrival are progression of the same event, so IV thrombolysis is outside its window.

Basilar artery occlusion within 24 hours of symptom onset with NIHSS 22, pre-stroke mRS 0 and PC-ASPECTS 7 meets the class 1 indication for thrombectomy (AHA/ASA 2026 section 4.7.3); BAOCHE showed benefit between 6 and 24 hours.
Headache, dizziness and blurred vision followed hours later by a stepwise brainstem decline is the typical prodrome of vertebrobasilar occlusion.

Right horizontal gaze palsy not overcome by the oculocephalic maneuver, right facial weakness and left hemiparesis localise to the right pontine tegmentum and basis (Foville syndrome); the mild right limb weakness and bilateral extensor plantars show extension across the midline, and the reduced consciousness reflects brainstem ischaemia from the basilar occlusion.

Pregnancy does not exclude thrombectomy; CT and iodinated contrast are not withheld when they decide reperfusion, gadolinium is avoided, and antithrombotic choices follow the ESO 2022 guideline on stroke in women (low-dose aspirin or LMWH; no warfarin, DOAC or statin).
Protein S activity falls physiologically in pregnancy and protein C and S can be consumed in acute thrombosis: the low values are repeated after delivery, not acted on now.
Pregnancy is a hypercoagulable state with elevated stroke risk; CVST, PRES, and arterial stroke must all be considered

patient.history_present_illness: Ms. Priya Nair is a 33-year-old right-handed woman, currently at 15 weeks and 5 days of gestation in her second pregnancy (primiparous, one prior cesarean delivery), who was brought to the emergency department by her husband after acute onset of bilateral frontotemporal headache associated with dizziness and blurred vision approximately 18 hours prior to presentation. She initially attributed her symptoms to pregnancy-related fatigue and rested at home. Over the next several hours, she developed two episodes of non-projectile, non-bloody vomiting. Her husband reports that approximately 6 hours ago, she became progressively less responsive, began producing incomprehensible speech instead of her usual fluent communication, and then suddenly developed weakness in her left arm that rapidly progressed to involve her left leg. He immediately brought her to the emergency department. On arrival, the patient appeared drowsy and distressed, making unintelligible vocalizations but unable to communicate meaningfully. She was moving her right extremities spontaneously but had minimal movement of the left arm and reduced movement of the left leg. There was no history of head trauma, seizure activity, urinary incontinence, chest pain, shortness of breath, palpitations, or vaginal bleeding. She has no prior history of neurological symptoms, migraines, or thromboembolic events. Her pregnancy has been uncomplicated to date, with normal first-trimester screening and ultrasound. She has no known vascular risk factors aside from the hypercoagulable state of pregnancy. She was last known well approximately 18 hours before arrival, before the headache, dizziness and blurred vision began; the decline in responsiveness and the left-sided weakness began about 6 hours before arrival. She was fully independent and working before this illness.
